item.description: UFT: 75-franc surcharge deemed unjustified Bus delay, then an alternative route The story begins with the Küsnacht-Rafz journey The case
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - UFT: 75-franc surcharge deemed unjustified - A bus delay, then an alternative route - The case begins with the Küsnacht-Rafz journey - The case may affect other travelers
## Key facts - Penalty → 75 francs - Zone surcharge → 1,10 francs - Route → Küsnacht-Rafz - Missed connection → Zurich Stadelhofen - Contested rule → T600 - Letter from ZVV → October 7 - FOT decision → unjustified surcharge - Outcome → no payment and cancellation of the registration
In a letter dated October 7, ZVV informed Fierz that he would not be required to make any payment and that his entry in the register of travelers without a valid ticket would be deleted. The communication came after months of complaints and after the Federal Office of Transport had deemed the contested surcharge unjustified.
### The interrupted journey
The story dates back to last spring. The pensioner from the Canton of Zurich was traveling with a friend from Küsnacht to Rafz for an outing, using public transport. A delayed bus caused the two to miss their connection at Zurich Stadelhofen. To reach their destination, they took the first available connection.
Unaware that they had crossed an additional fare zone, they should have paid 1,10 francs for that leg. Instead, the inspection ended with a penalty of 75 francs and their entry in the register of travelers without a valid ticket.
> “I felt treated like a criminal.”
### The dispute over the route
Fierz contested the penalty. He argued that the change of route was not his fault, but that of the public transport companies, and pointed out that the FFS app itself had suggested the alternative connection. His objection was also more general: in his view, one cannot expect every traveler to know all the fare zones.
At first, FFS customer service deducted 40 francs from the surcharge, leaving 35 francs to be paid in addition to the entry in the register. ZVV and the public transport conciliation body nevertheless rejected the objections. The dispute centered on provision T600, according to which, if a train is delayed or canceled, the holder of a valid ticket may use the next suitable connection, even via a different route, without paying a price difference. Fierz saw this as confirmation that he had acted correctly, while FFS and the conciliation body maintained that the connection could not cross additional fare zones. As a civil lawsuit appeared imminent, ZVV sought the opinion of the FOT, which overturned the previous decisions. Fierz nevertheless intends to pursue the civil lawsuit to obtain compensation. The practical significance of the decision lies not only in the difference between 1,10 and 75 francs. The case lays out three distinct levels: the price of the zone crossed, the surcharge imposed during the inspection and the entry in the register of travelers without a valid transport ticket. The 40-franc reduction granted by FFS had eliminated neither the 35-franc balance nor the entry. UFT's ruling changed both outcomes for Fierz.
### Four readings of the same rule
| Element | Reading emerging from the case | |---|---| | Valid ticket | Provision T600 covers the appropriate subsequent connection and, in certain cases, a different route without a price difference. | | Alternative route | Fierz linked it to the bus delay and the missed connection. | | FFS and conciliation | An appropriate connection, according to their interpretation, should not pass through additional fare zones. | | UFT | The surcharge applied in the specific case was deemed unjustified. |
The practical issue is therefore the notion of an appropriate connection. The T600 provision, as reported in the source, concerns the delay or cancellation of a train and recognizes the possibility of continuing with the next appropriate connection. The dispute arose from how this rule was to be interpreted in the case of an alternative route that crossed an additional zone.
In the specific case, the change was not presented as a choice to save money or modify the journey. It followed a bus delay, a missed connection at Zurich Stadelhofen and the suggestion from the FFS app. Fierz's position therefore linked the change of zone to a situation imposed by the service. The opposing position, on the other hand, separated the validity of the ticket from the possibility of crossing additional fare zones.
This contrast explains why a surcharge of 1,10 francs led to a broader dispute. The issue was not only the cost of the zone, but whether that cost could be charged after a route change caused by the delay.
The source indicates that the decision could also have consequences for other travelers. UFT, Alliance SwissPass and Unione dei trasporti pubblici will discuss the concrete procedures for applying it. The indicated next step is therefore the move from the decision in the individual case to defining the procedures for its application. Any compensation, by contrast, remains the subject of the civil case that the pensioner intends to pursue. To reconstruct the case in practical terms, the documented sequence does not begin with the final decision, but with the challenge to the inspection. There are five steps.
### The documented sequence
1. **Change of route.** A bus delay caused Fierz and his friend to miss their connection at Zurich Stadelhofen. The two took the first available connection to reach Rafz and crossed an additional fare zone.
2. Contestation of the penalty. The pensioner disputed the 75 francs, arguing that the change was not his fault. He also pointed out that the FFS app had suggested precisely the alternative connection.
3. Subsequent complaints. FFS customer service reduced the surcharge by 40 francs, but left 35 francs to pay and the entry in the register. ZVV and the conciliation body for public transport also initially rejected the objections.
4. Assessment by the federal authority. Faced with the prospect of a civil lawsuit, ZVV requested an assessment from the Federal Office of Transport, identified by the source as the competent supervisory authority.
5. Outcome of the decision. After the FOT's ruling, ZVV's letter of October 7 communicated that Fierz would not have to pay anything and that the entry would be deleted. The pensioner nevertheless wants to continue the civil lawsuit to obtain compensation.
The sequence separates two results that should not be confused. The decision communicated by ZVV concerns the surcharge and the register of travelers without a valid ticket. The claim for compensation, on the other hand, follows a separate civil route, which Fierz does not intend to abandon.
The chronology also helps to understand the case: the journey took place last spring, the complaints continued for months, and the decisive communication arrived on October 7. The source adds that the discussion on the practical application will involve UFT, Alliance SwissPass and Unione dei trasporti pubblici.

## Key facts - SSR survey → published on October 17, 2026 - UDC → almost 30% of voting intentions - Vote on war materiel → November 29 - Glaciers → Adula and Grauhorn are no longer connected - Solar Express → law adopted four years ago - Parliament → cannot table a motion of no confidence - Weapons at home → comprehensive data lacking - Swiss glaciers → one-fifth disappeared in five years
On October 17, 2026, the content dedicated to the week's Swiss current affairs presents a first SSR poll one year before the federal elections. The source does not suggest major political upheavals.
On October 16, another item describes a strengthening of polarization. The UDC leads the race and, with almost 30% of voting intentions, consolidates its position as Switzerland's largest party. The left is gaining ground, while the center-right parties are losing ground.
On the same day, the environmental dossier moves to Ticino. For the first time, the glaciers of Adula and Grauhorn are reported to be separated. The trip with experts from the canton serves to measure the effects of a changing climate. The report's title warns: «In a few years there will be no more glaciers in Ticino».
On October 14, the Solar Express project is presented as a promise that is still difficult to fulfill. The law was intended to accelerate the construction of alpine solar installations in Switzerland, but four years after its adoption, photovoltaics is still struggling to gain a foothold in the mountains.
### Institutional and international issues
Two items published on October 13 concern the functioning of the state and war materiel. The Swiss Parliament does not have the power to table a motion of no confidence against the Government. The source notes that this peculiarity, apparently undemocratic, also has some advantages.
On the same day, the Swiss population is called to the polls on November 29 to vote on a controversial proposal to amend the law on war materiel, aimed at easing its restrictions. On October 7, by contrast, the Swiss Government expressed its desire to establish a security partnership with the European Union, leaving open the question of whether the EU is willing to do the same. An item from October 6 also recalls that, while maintaining close ties with the EU, Switzerland does not intend to join it.
The review completes the picture with the issue of weapons available in homes: comprehensive data are lacking, and a motion calls on the Government to fill this gap. Finally, on October 2, the assessment of Swiss glaciers indicates that in 2026, summer heatwaves and scant winter snowfall led to the disappearance of dozens of glaciers. ## The practical reading of the dossiers
For those who live or work in Switzerland, the roundup should be read by separating the dossiers that are still open from the situations already described. This week's news do not amount to a single national decision: they bring together politics, institutions, security, relations with the EU, energy, and the environment.
The first point concerns the electoral calendar. The SSR poll captures voting intentions one year before the federal elections. The nearly 30% attributed to the SVP, the growth of the left, and the loss of support for center-right parties describe a shift in the balance of power indicated by the source, but do not constitute the election result. For the reader, the distinction prevents a political poll from being turned into a definitive prediction.
| Dossier | Distinction to maintain | |---|---| | Politics | Voting intentions and election result | | Weapons | Easing of the law and data on weapons in homes | | EU | Security partnership and membership in the European Union | | Environment | Alpine solar installations and glacier measurements |
The second point concerns institutions. The report on the no-confidence motion does not announce a new vote: it explains that Parliament cannot put forward that motion against the Government. The source also points to possible advantages of this approach. The issue therefore concerns the functioning of the Confederation and not a change already submitted to a popular vote.
The weapons dossier also requires precision. On November 29, the public will vote on easing the law on war materiel; separately, a motion asks the Government to address the lack of comprehensive data on weapons in homes. These are two different matters, and the source does not assign a decision date to the motion.
### Energy, ice and relations with Europe
At the European level, a security partnership and EU membership are not the same question: the Government wants the former, while Switzerland does not want to become a member of the EU. On the environmental front, the before-and-after comparison is explicit for Solar Express: the law aimed to accelerate alpine solar installations, but after four years photovoltaic power is still struggling to gain ground in the mountains. Measurements of Adula, Grauhorn, and the other glaciers add the cantonal and alpine dimension. The source does not quantify effects on wages, prices, or the cost of living; it is therefore not possible to derive precise amounts or economic consequences from these articles. ## A reading procedure for the week
To turn the roundup into a useful brief, it is advisable to proceed step by step and not merge together news items concerning different subjects.
1. Mark November 29 as the date of the Swiss population's vote on easing the law on war materiel. It is the clearest operational date indicated by the source.
2. Open two separate entries for the weapons issue. In the first, enter the vote on the law; in the second, note the motion calling on the Government to fill the lack of comprehensive data on weapons in homes. Do not assign the date of the vote on the law to the motion.
3. Record the SSR poll with the wording voting intentions and with the reference to one year before the federal elections. The UDC's nearly 30%, the left's growth, and the loss of support for center-right parties must be retained as elements of the poll, not as an already-decided election outcome.
4. For the European dossier, use two separate lines: security partnership and relationship with the European Union. The first concerns the Swiss Government's willingness; the second includes the question about the EU's willingness and the rejection of Swiss accession.
5. For the environment and energy, build a comparison between the objective and the observed situation. Solar Express aimed to accelerate alpine solar installations, while photovoltaics is still struggling in the mountains. For glaciers, note separately the measurement by the canton's experts and the assessment concerning the Swiss Alps.
The final check consists in not adding data that the source does not provide. The sentence about the glaciers in Ticino says «in a few years», not a precise date. The news about weapons in the home refers to an information gap, not a new count. The European dossier asks a question about the EU's willingness; it does not announce an agreement. This framework makes it possible to follow the Swiss political calendar without confusing a poll, a motion, a law, a measurement, and a partnership.

## TL;DR - 30'000 m³ of reserves can be used - Authorized withdrawals from October 15 to November 1st - The authorized quota is 6,5% of the available amount - Swiss supply remains guaranteed
## Key facts - Location → Zurich-Kloten Airport - Volume → 30'000 cubic metres - Period → from October 15 to November 1 - Quota → 6,5% of what is available - Kerosene management → UBAG
30'000 cubic metres of kerosene may be withdrawn from mandatory reserves. The country's Delegate for Economic Supply authorized its use on Thursday from October 15 to November 1. The quantity corresponds to 6,5% of what is available.
The intervention is linked to interruptions and considerable delays in international rail transport, especially from Germany. The reported risk is that Zurich Airport could run short of kerosene. The Confederation explains that trains are also failing to keep to schedule because large quantities of goods have been transferred to rail after river transport became impossible due to the low water level of the Rhine.
### What is guaranteed and what is under pressure The same communication specifies that Swiss supplies of petrol, diesel and heating oil have deteriorated compared with the previous week, but remain guaranteed. For people living in Switzerland, the wording therefore distinguishes between a deterioration in the situation and an interruption in availability: the note does not announce that these products have run out.
Asked about this, Zurich-Kloten Airport stated that, for now, departing aircraft are not subject to refuelling restrictions. UBAG manages the kerosene and deals with a total of nine external suppliers, including Socar, BP and Shell. All the fuel arrives at the airport by rail.
The airport management is not commenting on shortages at international level and refers to the airlines regarding refuelling flights bound for Frankfurt. Germany's main airport, which serves as a hub for Lufthansa, Swiss's parent company, is also experiencing difficulties. Lufthansa does not anticipate cancellations, but has invited crews bound for Frankfurt to depart with fuller tanks. ## The operational bottleneck is transport
The decision on reserves must be read together with one fact: all of the kerosene for Zurich-Kloten reaches the airport by rail. For this reason, disruptions to rail traffic directly affect the airport's fuel supply. The source links the difficulty to international delays, particularly from Germany, and to the diversion to rail of large quantities of goods that could no longer travel by river.
A proper reading avoids confusing three different elements: the availability of reserves, the punctuality of trains and the status of aircraft refuelling. The communication presents them in the same episode, but does not describe them in the same way.
### The data to distinguish
| Area | Stated status | Practical interpretation | |---|---|---| | Mandatory reserves | 30'000 m³, equal to 6,5% of the available amount | Measure limited to the period indicated | | Rail transport | Disruptions and delays, especially from Germany | Arrival route for all kerosene | | Refuelling at Zurich-Kloten | No restrictions currently in force | Situation of departing aircraft | | Energy products in Switzerland | Worse than the previous week, but guaranteed | Gasoline, diesel and heating oil | | Frankfurt | Difficult situation and no cancellations expected by Lufthansa | Operational reference for airlines |
The relationship between the Rhine and rail is the most relevant point for understanding the origin of the logistical pressure. The river's low water level made it impossible to transport large quantities by river; those goods were transferred to rail, while the trains are not keeping to schedule. Zurich Airport is therefore exposed to a delivery problem, despite no declared restrictions on refuelling departing aircraft.
For the Swiss market, the message remains cautious: the availability of gasoline, diesel and heating oil has worsened, but the Confederation still describes it as guaranteed. For travellers, however, the source distinguishes Zurich from Frankfurt: the Swiss airport reports no restrictions, while for Frankfurt the airlines are the point of reference, and Lufthansa recommends fuller fuel tanks for crews. ## How to navigate
To turn the news into a concrete check, the first step is to establish which situation is being observed: a flight departing from Zurich-Kloten, a flight bound for Frankfurt or the supply of petrol, diesel and heating oil in Switzerland. These are areas linked by logistics, but the source provides different information for each.
### Four practical checks
1. For a flight departing from Zurich-Kloten, the airport's communication indicates that, for now, departing aircraft can be refueled without restrictions.
2. For a destination in Frankfurt, the airport management refers passengers to the airlines. Lufthansa does not expect cancellations, but has recommended that crews heading to the German city depart with fuller tanks.
3. If the interest concerns consumption in Switzerland, the three products mentioned in the note must be distinguished: petrol, diesel and heating oil. Their availability has worsened compared with the previous week, but remains guaranteed.
4. If one wants to track the duration of the measure concerning stocks, the dates to note are October 15 and November 1. The authorized volume is 30'000 cubic meters, equal to 6,5% of what is available.
The data on the full supply chain completes the operational picture. UBAG manages kerosene and turns to nine external suppliers, including Socar, BP and Shell; all the fuel reaches the airport by rail. International delays, especially from Germany, and the low level of the Rhine explain why transport punctuality is the point to monitor.
The source does not describe a general stoppage of flights from Zurich. Instead, it distinguishes between refueling currently without restrictions at the airport, difficulties in Frankfurt and Swiss energy supply that is still guaranteed.
